A court may not estimate a deductible expense unless the taxpayer presents a sufficient evidentiary basis on which an estimate can be made

Section 274(d) imposes strict substantiation requirements on travel expenses, requiring the taxpayer to substantiate the amount, time and place, business purpose, and business relationship of the expense
If a taxpayer cannot provide adequate records or sufficient evidence corroborating their statement, the court will not allow an estimate of the expenses

verdicts.why: Sources state adequate records require contemporaneous account book, diary, log, and documentary evidence like receipts.
T.C. Memo 2025-26 states reconstruction allowed only after proving adequate records were lost to fire, flood, or casualty.
T.C. Memo 2026-34 states court will not estimate expense unless taxpayer presents sufficient evidentiary basis.
T.C. Memo 2026-34 cites Section 274(d) requiring substantiation of amount, time/place, business purpose, and business relationship.
T.C. Memo 2026-34 states Cohan doctrine cannot be invoked for section 274(d) expenses lacking adequate substantiation.

claims: Transportation expenses incurred by an employee for commuting between home and the office are nondeductible commuting expenses
No deduction is allowed for any expense incurred for providing transportation to an employee in connection with travel between the employee's residence and place of employment

verdicts.why: IRS Pub 463 states transportation expenses between home and first business contact are nondeductible commuting expenses.
26 U.S.C. § 274(l) prohibits deductions for transportation between residence and place of employment, with limited exceptions.

claims: The taxpayer generally bears the burden of proof for insolvency in cancellation of debt income cases
If the IRS raises the issue of cancellation of debt income, the IRS must prove that the taxpayer was solvent

verdicts.why: Sources show burden allocation depends on whether IRS raised the issue in original NOD or later; general rule not supported.
T.C. Memo 2024-79 holds that when IRS raises COD income for first time, IRS bears burden to prove taxpayer was solvent.

claims: A cash-method taxpayer cannot deduct unpaid fees as worthless debts because such debts have not been included in income
For a debt to be deductible as a bad debt, it must have been previously reported in income
A cash basis taxpayer does not include unpaid fees in income before they are actually or constructively received
A debt arising from receivables is deemed to be an enforceable obligation only if the income it represents has been included in the taxpayer's return
The client operates as a cash-method taxpayer

verdicts.why: Sources state unpaid fees of cash-basis taxpayers are not included in income and thus cannot be deducted as bad debts under § 166.
Treasury Reg. § 1.166-1(c) and (e) require income to have been previously reported for bad debt deduction.
Sources cite §§ 451, 461 and regulations establishing cash-basis taxpayers only include income when actually or constructively received.
Treas. Reg. § 1.166-1(c) states debt is deemed enforceable only to extent income was included in prior returns.
Sources do not state the client operates as cash-method; question only states this as a premise to answer.

claims: A taxpayer may challenge the existence or amount of the underlying tax liability at a collection hearing only if the taxpayer did not receive a notice of deficiency or did not otherwise have an opportunity to challenge the underlying liability
The term underlying liability includes the tax reported on a return prepared by the taxpayer
A Letter 1153 that is not received and not deliberately refused by the taxpayer does not constitute an opportunity to dispute underlying liability
The IRS is required to provide the taxpayer with notice of trust fund recovery penalties before assessment
If the taxpayer did not receive the Letter 1153 proposing the penalty, the taxpayer may have grounds to dispute the penalty at the collection hearing

verdicts.why: Section 6330(c)(2)(B) states taxpayer may challenge underlying liability only if did not receive notice of deficiency or otherwise have opportunity to challenge.
T.C. Memo 2010-140 at *6-7 states underlying liability includes tax reported on return prepared by taxpayer.
T.C. Memo 2010-140 at *11-12 states Letter 1153 not received and not deliberately refused does not constitute opportunity to dispute.
T.C. Memo 2010-140 at *10-11 states Commissioner required to provide notice of trust fund recovery penalties before assessment under section 6672(b)(1).
T.C. Memo 2010-140 at *14-15 holds taxpayer who did not receive Letter 1153 had prior opportunity to dispute penalties at collection hearing.

claims: The client has $60,000 of income
Gross income includes compensation for services, which includes sales commissions
The $40,000 that was kept to cancel the rent owed is considered income to the client
The offset of the rent owed does not negate the income recognition from the commission earned
The amount of the commission that was offset against the debt does not reduce the income recognized from the commission

verdicts.why: Sources show client has $60,000 commission income, but one case distinguishes between full commission earned and amount reported as income.
26 U.S.C. § 61(a) broadly defines gross income to include compensation for services.
T.C. Memo. 2001-252 holds that offsetting commission against rent debt constitutes taxable income to the employee.
T.C. Memo. 2001-252 states the fact that rent was paid from commission is irrelevant to income recognition.
T.C. Memo. 2001-252 holds petitioner realized $60,500 commission income despite $40,500 offset against debt owed.

claims: The Eleventh Circuit concluded that the IRS satisfies section 6751(b) so long as a supervisor approves an initial determination of a penalty assessment before the IRS assesses those penalties
Written supervisory approval is not required to take any specific form
Supervisory approval must generally be obtained no later than the date on which the IRS issues the deficiency notice
Supervisory approval must generally be obtained no later than the date on which the IRS formally communicates to the taxpayer the Examination Division's determination to assert a penalty
As long as the approval is secured before the penalties are assessed, it is considered timely

verdicts.why: Kroner v. Commissioner, 48 F.4th 1272 (11th Cir. 2022) explicitly states this conclusion.
T.C. Memo. 2023-5 cites Palmolive Bldg. Invs., LLC v. Commissioner for this principle.
T.C. Memo. 2023-5 at *15 lists this as one of two general timing requirements.
T.C. Memo. 2023-5 at *15 lists this as the alternative general timing requirement.
Eleventh Circuit standard in Kroner requires approval before assessment, which applies to this appealable case.

claims: A taxpayer may avoid penalties for disallowed deductions if they can demonstrate reasonable reliance on professional advice.
To successfully claim reliance on professional advice, the adviser must be independent and not affiliated with the promoter of the transaction.
Reliance on advice from a promoter or someone with a conflict of interest is generally considered unreasonable and does not protect against penalties.
If the promoter provided the advice and had a financial interest in the welfare benefit plan, reliance on that advice would likely be deemed unreasonable.

verdicts.why: Sources indicate reliance on professional advice can avoid penalties, but only under specific conditions regarding independence.
Multiple sources explicitly state the adviser must be independent and not affiliated with or have conflict of interest with promoter.
Sources repeatedly hold reliance on promoter or conflicted adviser advice is unreasonable and does not protect against penalties.
Sources show reliance on promoter advice with financial interest in transaction is deemed unreasonable and fails to avoid penalties.

claims: Shareholders of S corporations can receive a distribution of assets from one S corporation and then contribute those assets into another S corporation to increase their bases in the latter
A distribution of assets from one S corporation followed by a contribution to another S corporation decreases the shareholders' bases in the distributing S corporation
A distribution of assets from one S corporation followed by a contribution to another S corporation increases the shareholders' bases in the receiving S corporation
The transactions must actually occur for the basis increase to be valid
The existence of a close relationship between S corporations does not preclude this arrangement as long as the transactions are bona fide

verdicts.why: T.C. Memo. 2012-160 explicitly holds shareholders are not prohibited from receiving distributions from one S corp and contributing to another to increase bases.
T.C. Memo. 2012-160 states distribution decreases shareholders' bases in the distributing S corporation.
T.C. Memo. 2012-160 states contribution increases shareholders' bases in receiving S corporation.
T.C. Memo. 2012-160 requires underlying distributions and contributions actually occurred for validity.
T.C. Memo. 2012-160 states close relationship does not preclude arrangement if transactions actually occurred and are bona fide.

claims: The taxpayer generally bears the burden of proving that the IRS's determinations in a notice of deficiency are erroneous
The burden of proof may shift to the IRS if the taxpayer introduces credible evidence and satisfies certain conditions
One condition for shifting the burden of proof to the IRS is that the taxpayer must have cooperated with reasonable requests by the IRS for witnesses, information, documents, meetings, and interviews
Failure to cooperate with the IRS during an audit counts heavily against a taxpayer's attempt to shift the burden of proof

verdicts.why: 26 U.S.C. § 7491 and multiple Tax Court cases confirm taxpayer bears initial burden to prove deficiency determinations erroneous.
26 U.S.C. § 7491(a)(1)-(2) explicitly provides burden shifts if taxpayer introduces credible evidence and meets additional conditions.
26 U.S.C. § 7491(a)(2)(B) requires taxpayer cooperation with reasonable IRS requests for witnesses, information, documents, meetings, and interviews.
T.C. Memo. 2022-83 states failure to cooperate and maintain records counts heavily against taxpayer's burden-shifting attempt.

claims: An understatement of income tax is considered substantial if it exceeds the greater of 10% of the tax required to be shown on the return or $5,000
The client did not reconstruct records after they were destroyed in a flood
A taxpayer may be liable for the accuracy-related penalty due to a substantial understatement of income tax if they fail to maintain sufficient records to substantiate the items in question
The absence of reconstructed records indicates a lack of reasonable effort to substantiate the deductions claimed
The client is liable for the substantial understatement penalty under Internal Revenue Code section 6662

verdicts.why: T.C. Memo. 2013-280 defines substantial understatement as exceeding greater of 10% of tax required to be shown or $5,000.
Question states client's records were destroyed in flood and he didn't reconstruct them.
T.C. Memo. 2013-280 states taxpayer is negligent if failing to maintain sufficient records to substantiate items.
T.C. Memo. 2026-65 upheld penalty where taxpayer failed to make reasonable effort to reconstruct records after flood.
Sources show conditions for liability but don't address whether reasonable cause/good faith exception applies here.

claims: A client can deduct rental expenses on Schedule E if rental days exceed personal use days
Rental expense deductions are limited if rental days do not exceed personal use days
A dwelling unit is considered a home if it is used for personal purposes
Whether a dwelling unit is considered a home depends on the number of days it is used for personal purposes compared to rental purposes
If a dwelling unit is used as a home and rented for 15 days or more during the year, expenses must be divided between rental use and personal use
If a dwelling unit is used as a home and rented for 15 days or more during the year, only rental expenses can be deducted on Schedule E
If a taxpayer has personal use of a dwelling unit, deductible rental expenses are limited based on the ratio of days rented to total days used

verdicts.why: Sources require expense division based on days rented vs. total days used, not just exceeding personal use days.
IRC 280A(e)(1) limits deductible rental expenses to ratio of rental days to total days used.
IRS Pub 527 states if dwelling has personal use, it is treated as a home for purposes of expense division.
Sources indicate personal use alone establishes home status; comparison of days is not the determining factor.
IRS Pub 527 explicitly states if rented 15+ days and used as home, expenses must be divided between uses.
IRS Pub 527 states only rental expenses may be deducted on Schedule E when dwelling has personal use.
IRC 280A(e)(1) limits rental deductions to amount bearing same ratio as rental days to total days used.

claims: Section 530 of the Revenue Act of 1978 provides relief from employment taxes for employers who incorrectly classify workers as independent contractors instead of employees, provided certain requirements are met
To qualify for section 530 relief, a taxpayer must not have treated the worker as an employee for any period
To qualify for section 530 relief, a taxpayer must have consistently filed all required federal tax returns on a basis consistent with treating the worker as not being an employee
To qualify for section 530 relief, a taxpayer must have had a reasonable basis for not treating the worker as an employee
To qualify for section 530 relief, a taxpayer must not have treated any individual holding a substantially similar position as an employee
The IRS's classification of payments as wages instead of royalties indicates that the payments to the owner-employee are considered wages for employment tax purposes
If payments are classified as wages, section 530 relief may not be available if the taxpayer treated any individual in a substantially similar position as an employee

verdicts.why: Section 530 affords relief from employment taxes when taxpayer did not treat individual as employee, with certain requirements met.
Section 530(a)(1)(A) requires taxpayer did not treat individual as employee for any period for employment tax purposes.
Section 530(a)(1)(B) requires federal tax returns filed consistently with treatment of individual as not being employee.
Section 530(a)(2) requires taxpayer had reasonable basis for not treating worker as employee.
Section 530(a)(3) limits relief if taxpayer treated individual in substantially similar position as employee.
121 T.C. No. 6 sustained IRS determination that payments to owner were wages, not royalties for employment tax purposes.
If payments are wages and substantive consistency requirement violated, section 530 relief unavailable under section 530(a)(3).

claims: Expenses related to writing and research activities may be deductible if they are ordinary and necessary expenses incurred in the trade or business of writing
If the writing activity does not have a profit objective, the IRS may disallow the deductions for expenses related to that activity
The lack of income over several years may indicate that the writing activity is not engaged in for profit
A lack of income over several years could limit the ability to deduct expenses related to a writing activity
A taxpayer must demonstrate a profit motive to deduct expenses related to a business activity
Consistent losses may raise questions about whether a taxpayer has a profit motive

verdicts.why: 26 U.S.C. § 263A(h)(2) covers qualified creative expenses for writers that would be allowable deductions.
T.C. Memo. 2010-144 discusses profit objective as factor in determining deductibility of writing expenses.
T.C. Memo. 2024-75 shows taxpayer claiming losses for ~26 years with first profit in 2022, supporting this claim.
T.C. Memo. 2024-75 implies lack of income limits deductions; taxpayer's consistent losses raised deductibility questions.
T.C. Memo. 2010-144 at *21-22 explicitly discusses profit objective as required factor for business deductions.
T.C. Memo. 2024-75 shows consistent losses raised profit motive questions; T.C. Memo. 2010-144 discusses profit objective factor.

claims: Net earnings from self-employment are defined as the gross income derived from carrying on any trade or business less allowable deductions attributable to that trade or business
The determination of whether income is subject to self-employment tax depends on whether the individual has an employee or independent contractor relationship with the payer
If off-duty police officers are considered independent contractors, their income from providing security services is subject to self-employment tax

verdicts.why: 26 U.S.C. § 1402(a) and T.C. Memo. 2024-49 directly define net earnings from self-employment as gross income from trade or business less allowable deductions.
T.C. Memo. 2012-343 explicitly states the resolution of self-employment tax liability turns on whether individual had employee or independent contractor relationship.
T.C. Memo. 2012-343 holds that off-duty police officer with independent contractor relationship is subject to self-employment tax on security service income.

claims: Interest credited to a certificate of deposit is generally included in gross income for the taxable year in which it is credited, regardless of whether it is withdrawn or subject to an early withdrawal penalty
The potential for an early withdrawal penalty does not prevent the taxpayer from being in constructive receipt of the interest income
Income is constructively received when it is credited to the taxpayer's account and available for withdrawal, even if there are penalties for early withdrawal

verdicts.why: T.C. Memo 2010-190 holds taxpayer must report interest credited to CD accounts even though subject to early withdrawal penalty.
T.C. Memo 2010-190 finds early withdrawal penalty is not substantial limitation preventing constructive receipt of interest income.
26 CFR 1.451-2(a) establishes constructive receipt when income credited and available; early withdrawal penalties not listed as substantial restrictions.

claims: The client may qualify for relief under Internal Revenue Code section 6015(b) if she can establish she did not know and had no reason to know about the disallowed deductions
It is inequitable to hold the client liable for the deficiency if certain conditions are met under Internal Revenue Code section 6015(b)
The client signed joint returns with her husband for a taxable year
Under Internal Revenue Code section 6015(b), a spouse must establish that in signing the return, she did not know and had no reason to know that there was an understatement
The client had no involvement in her husband's business
A lack of involvement in a spouse's business supports a claim of not knowing about disallowed deductions from that business

Under Internal Revenue Code section 6015(b), it must be determined whether it is inequitable to hold the client liable for the deficiency in tax attributable to the understatement, taking into account all facts and circumstances

verdicts.why: Section 6015(b) allows relief if spouse didn't know/have reason to know of understatement and elects within 2 years of collection activities.
Section 6015(b)(1)(D) requires that taking into account all facts and circumstances, it be inequitable to hold spouse liable.
The question states client signed joint returns; section 6015(b)(1)(A) requires a joint return.
Section 6015(b)(1)(C) explicitly requires spouse establish she did not know and had no reason to know of understatement.
Question states client had no involvement in husband's business.
T.C. Memo 2009-201 and other cases recognize lack of involvement as supporting no knowledge of disallowed deductions.
Section 6015(b)(1)(D) explicitly requires considering all facts and circumstances regarding inequitability.

claims: A 40% gross valuation misstatement penalty applies
The claimed value exceeds the correct value by more than 200%
An excess of claimed value over correct value by more than 200% constitutes a gross valuation misstatement
A gross valuation misstatement penalty of 40% applies to the portion of the underpayment attributable to the overvaluation of the conservation easement
The taxpayer cannot demonstrate reasonable cause or good faith as a defense against the gross valuation misstatement penalty

verdicts.why: Sources show 40% gross valuation misstatement penalties applied in multiple conservation easement cases.
Client claimed $10M, IRS valued at $3M; $10M exceeds $3M by 233%, more than 200%.
§6662(h)(2)(A)(i) defines gross valuation misstatement as claimed value ≥200% of correct value.
Multiple sources confirm 40% penalty applies to underpayment portions from conservation easement overvaluation.
§6664(c)(3) states reasonable cause defense unavailable for gross valuation misstatements on charitable property.

claims: The IRS standard mileage rate for business use of an automobile for 2025 is 70 cents per mile

verdicts.why: IRS Pub 334 (2025) and IRS Pub 527 (2025) both explicitly state the business standard mileage rate for 2025 is 70 cents per mile.

claims: For taxable years beginning in a calendar year after 1974, the maximum self-employment income equals the contribution and benefit base effective for such calendar year
The contribution and benefit base is determined under section 230 of the Social Security Act

verdicts.why: 26 CFR 1.1402(b)-1(b)(1)(i) states this directly for taxable years after 1974.
Both 26 CFR 1.1402(b)-1(b)(1)(i) and 26 U.S.C. § 1402(b) reference section 230 of the Social Security Act for determining contribution and benefit base.

claims: Federal bonus depreciation provisions allow for an additional first year depreciation deduction for qualified property
Qualified property under bonus depreciation includes MACRS property with a recovery period of 20 years or less
Qualified property under bonus depreciation includes computer software
Qualified property under bonus depreciation includes water utility property
Qualified property under bonus depreciation includes qualified leasehold improvement property

verdicts.why: Sources reference 'additional first year depreciation deduction' for qualified property throughout multiple regulations.
26 CFR 1.168(k)-1(b)(2)(i)(A) states MACRS property with 20 years or less recovery period meets qualified property requirements.
26 CFR 1.168(k)-1(b)(2)(i)(B) specifies computer software as defined in section 167(f)(1) qualifies.
26 CFR 1.168(k)-1(b)(2)(i)(C) identifies water utility property under section 168(e)(5) as qualified property.
26 CFR 1.168(k)-1(b)(2)(i)(D) lists qualified leasehold improvement property as meeting qualified property requirements.

claims: The IRS currently takes up to 16 weeks to process amended returns
It can take up to 3 weeks from the date an amended return is filed for it to show up in the IRS system

verdicts.why: IRS Pub 17 (2025) p. 131 states processing amended returns can take up to 16 weeks.
IRS Pub 17 (2025) p. 131 states it can take up to 3 weeks for amended return to show up in system.

claims: The IRS charges interest on underpayments based on the underpayment rate established under section 6621
The underpayment rate is the sum of the Federal short-term rate plus 3 percentage points
The Federal short-term rate for any month is determined by the Secretary in accordance with section 1274(d)

verdicts.why: 26 U.S.C. § 6654(a) establishes underpayment rate under section 6621 for individual underpayments.
26 U.S.C. § 6621(a)(2) states underpayment rate equals Federal short-term rate plus 3 percentage points.
26 U.S.C. § 6621(b)(3) states Federal short-term rate determined by Secretary per section 1274(d).

claims: The deduction for qualified tips is set to expire after December 31, 2028
No deduction is allowed under section 224 for any taxable year beginning after December 31, 2028

verdicts.why: 26 U.S.C. § 224(h) states no deduction allowed for taxable year beginning after December 31, 2028.
26 U.S.C. § 224(h) explicitly provides termination date of December 31, 2028.

claims: The penalty for a partnership that fails to file a franchise tax report at the prescribed time is $195 per month for each partner, up to 12 months
The penalty for a partnership can be waived if the failure is due to reasonable cause
The penalty for an S corporation that fails to file a franchise tax report at the prescribed time is $195 per month for each shareholder, up to 12 months
The penalty for an S corporation can be waived if the failure is due to reasonable cause

verdicts.why: 26 U.S.C. § 6698(a)-(b) states partnership penalty is $195 multiplied by number of partners per month, up to 12 months.
26 U.S.C. § 6698(a) exempts partnerships from penalty if failure is due to reasonable cause.
26 U.S.C. § 6699(a)-(b) states S corporation penalty is $195 multiplied by number of shareholders per month, up to 12 months.
26 U.S.C. § 6699(a) exempts S corporations from penalty if failure is due to reasonable cause.

claims: For taxable years beginning after 2027, the dollar amount will be increased by the cost-of-living adjustment determined under section 1(f)(3)

verdicts.why: 26 U.S.C. § 179(b)(6)(A) states dollar amounts shall be increased by cost-of-living adjustment under section 1(f)(3) for taxable years beginning after 2025.

claims: A self-employed individual can deduct expenses for the part of their home used exclusively and regularly for business if they meet specific tests
One test for home office deduction is physically meeting with patients, clients, or customers on the premises
One test for home office deduction is that the use of the home is substantial and integral to the conduct of the business
Using a home for occasional meetings and telephone calls does not qualify for the home office deduction

verdicts.why: IRS Pub 587 states expenses for home used exclusively and regularly for business can be deducted if meeting specific tests.
IRS Pub 587 lists physically meeting with patients, clients, or customers on premises as first required test.
IRS Pub 587 lists their use being substantial and integral to business conduct as second required test.
IRS Pub 587 explicitly states occasional meetings and telephone calls will not qualify for deduction.

claims: Interest on a construction loan for a rental property must be capitalized under Section 263A(f) when it is paid or incurred during the production period
The production period begins on the first date that any physical production activity is performed, such as clearing, grading, or excavating land
The production period ends on the date that the property is placed into service and all production activities reasonably expected to be undertaken by the taxpayer are completed

verdicts.why: Section 263A(f) requires capitalization of interest for self-produced assets when paid or incurred during production period for real property.
Production period begins on first date physical production activity performed, e.g., clearing, grading, or excavating land.
Production period ends when property placed in service and all production activities reasonably expected completed.

claims: For tax year 2025, the maximum first-year depreciation deduction for passenger automobiles placed in service is $20,200 if the vehicle qualifies for the Code section 168(k) additional first-year depreciation deduction
To qualify for the 100% additional first-year depreciation deduction, a passenger automobile must be acquired after January 19, 2025
To qualify for the 100% additional first-year depreciation deduction, a passenger automobile must be used more than 50% in a qualified business use during the tax year
For tax year 2025, if a passenger automobile does not qualify for the Code section 168(k) additional first-year depreciation deduction, the maximum first-year depreciation deduction is $12,200

verdicts.why: IRS Pub 463 p.1 states first tax year limit is $20,200 for automobiles acquired after January 19, 2025, with 168(k) deduction.
IRS Pub 463 p.24 requires car be acquired after January 19, 2025 for 100% additional first-year depreciation deduction.
IRS Pub 463 p.24 requires car be used more than 50% in qualified business use during tax year for 100% deduction.
IRS Pub 463 p.24 states first tax year limit is $12,200 for automobiles without Code section 168(k) additional depreciation.
